utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May I introduce Marialejandra Moreno Mantilla, who is from Colombia and who has been assisting my team for the past five months. She is a lawyer who graduated from El Rosario University in Bogota. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Pack, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now I'd like to remind you of your evidence yesterday in response to my question about Mladic's words at the meeting on the 1st of July, 1994, at the Drina Corps command, which you attended. In answer to my question which related to that, to his words, "the enclave is not to survive but to disappear," one of the things you said was this, and I'm quoting from page 42626 of the transcript. You said: "I personally made efforts for them," and this was the Muslim civilian population in Srebrenica, "I personally made efforts for them to get water. I did that personally, myself. I made sure that people had water because I know quite well how much and what exactly that means." Do you remember your testimony to that effect yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You made sure, did you, that the Muslim civilian population in Srebrenica got their water?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Srebrenica get water, the civilians and the army both.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can I have, please, P05147?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, as it's coming up let me explain what this is. It's a document dated the 31st of May, 1993, after Srebrenica was declared a safe area. And you can see there, it's from your deputy, Milutin Skocajic and it's to the TG 1 command, for the attention of Colonel Vukota Vukovic or Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Urosevic [phoen]. It's marked urgent, to be submitted immediately. I'm going to read that first paragraph. You can follow it in B/C/S. "Lieutenant-Colonel Urosevic received a verbal order from the commander Colonel Milenko Zivanovic to demolish the water-tower and tank in the area of Zeleni Jadar (water supply system for Srebrenica). Since this has not been done so far, this task is to be executed immediately by June 1, 1993, at the latest, and it is to be presented to the public as if the Muslim forces did it." Reading on: "During the execution of the task, strictly take care of safety of personnel and our forces in order to prevent any consequences. Upon the execution of the task, inform this command in writing." You issued an order, General, to demolish the water supply system for Srebrenica, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the water supply system. Just the water-tower, which was in a ruinous state and served Muslims to supply Zeleni Jadar, whereas the pipes and water supply installations remained intact. That's my answer. And finally, this is not my order. Because you can't perceive this element, this water-tower, which was out of order anyway, and served as an observation point for various sabotage groups. The water supply installations themselves were in operation, which you can verify in the record because late Nikola Koljevic visited to see about that issue. So this is not an ad hoc story. A man from our top leadership came. This was settled, and he personally went to Jadar. There are probably records of that visit, but the point is that Srebrenica was not without water. Besides, Srebrenica has another reservoir which also could have been destroyed if anyone had wanted to destroy it, and that's on the Bojna hill. That's a supply of high quality fresh water, which went from the Serbian village of Viogor, that water installation was always carefully guarded, and I repeat there was not a single day that Srebrenica went without water. That's my response to this text you've shown me, which you can see has been abused.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you issue a verbal order "to demolish the water-tower and tank in the area of Zeleni Jadar (water supply system of Srebrenica)"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. Just to stop the water-tower from being used as an observation point by sabotage groups. And the water supply system had to be preserved, which was confirmed by the constant presence of water in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your aim, wasn't it, was to pass off responsibility for this action on to the Muslim forces and then to pass them off as deceitful when they came to blame you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could not be accepted that way, especially since I did not draft this text and did not sign it, and it's very awkward to discuss these details that were decided by two different people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, let's see how you followed it up, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have P05148?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Two different people who are both dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is an order, very urgent, signed by you, dated the 21st of June, 1993, and it's to Colonel Vukota Vukovic. You remember him from the last order. And it's to submit the data on the Muslim DTG that demolished the water supply system in Zeleni Jadar. "Since we need to inform highest UNPROFOR bodies about the barbaric act of the Muslim DTG when they demolished the water supply system in Zeleni Jadar and on this occasion directly confronted our forces, inform me about the following." And then you list the various things you need to -- the details -- wait, the details, wait, that you have to be provided in a false report by Vukovic; right? You required Vukovic to provide you with the means to deceive international actors, in writing, as to which party to the conflict was responsible for the destruction of the water supply at Zeleni Jadar; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, the water-tower of the water supply system which went from Zeleni Jadar to Srebrenica is far from the industrial complex, 1.7 kilometres. The industrial zone in Zeleni Jadar, the timber industry, the wood processing industry, that section was extremely threatened because we were not controlling it at that point and the truth is, and this is really a coincidence, that there was a rupture in the pipeline caused by a sabotage group. With all due respect, you should have read out this order in its entirety, see what I wrote: Submit identification data for these persons, if you are in possession of any. So that's really how it happened. We made an urgent intervention in order to let it be known that the water supply has to continue operating. If it had not been in our interest for the water supply system to continue operating, it would not have operated. You have different positions, but this is the real truth. Why? Because UNPROFOR, with all its forces, in addition to all its other tasks, had the task to control this axis. However, especially in the beginning, they did not move around much, and one day I even asked them to provide me with information as to their ability to deploy and to accomplish their missions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's go to P05148 -- 49, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, very shortly after you sent your order to Vukovic, you get the following manufactured report, the lie; right? Dated 21st June, timed at 1715 hours. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not legible but I can make it out. Now -- now I can read.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see it's addressed to you. And in the first paragraph, on 26 May at 2058 hours the Turks launched surprise violent attack and so it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And let's turn over, please, to the second page in the English, still the first page in the B/C/S, and we are looking at -- it's the third paragraph from the bottom, for the B/C/S, we are just looking at the third and fourth paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "On 27th May, the following day, during the meeting with UNPROFOR, I protested," and it goes on, "saying that they served as a shield to the Muslim terrorists to destroy the facilities without disturbances only to accuse us before the world for the so-called vandalism, just like they always do." And then at the end of the paragraph: "They replied positively to my claims, disgusted by Muslims' behaviour." Next paragraph: "During the two following meetings with UNPROFOR," in the context of criticising Muslims, et cetera, then he says, "I reiterated and emphasised that they are so cunning and evil" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Documents are missing on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They are coming. Just to confirm, this set of documents were admitted through bar table motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll have to check, Mr. President. They are certainly admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was reading the penultimate paragraph. I think I got to the last phrase: "... I reiterated and emphasised that they are so cunning and evil," the Muslims that is, "that they will commit the most horrible sabotages on structures, let alone what they would do to us Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So this, General, this is Vukovic reporting that he has already used the attack that you ordered to deceive UNPROFOR to communicate the lie that Muslim forces destroyed the water supply system for Srebrenica so that they could falsely accuse Serb forces of doing so; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, please, if you are using official reports of my subordinate commanders to portray them as false, in my view that's inappropriate. This UNPROFOR, those are not fictitious people. They were real people who confirmed that this was destroyed by the Muslims. Check with people who were there on the spot and who met with Vukovic, my representative, who was supposed to facilitate UNPROFOR's work. Let's not play games with these things. And how can you say that what my subordinate is writing to me is false? How could it be false when there was an official meeting between my representative and people from the UNPROFOR who were in charge of the Jadar area? Why don't you look for some evidence from UNPROFOR itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: General, you --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this is -- this leads nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: General, you issued the order. We've seen -- we've seen that. You don't deny that you issued the order to demolish the water system.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we also see this order, where the sabotage had already been carried out in that area. We see that order which you say is false. We can't work this way. We can't accept this manner. You show one order and treat it as false and another one that suits you is okay. But the truth is that a Muslim unit went through UNPROFOR lines and carried out this sabotage action, and at the same time, we were talking about the demilitarisation of that whole territory, whereas they went on launching attacks one after another. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, these documents were admitted via the Srebrenica bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's move on for the moment. Thank you, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The enclave is not to survive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Pack, do we have evidence when that water-tower was demolished?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The only evidence, and I'll stand corrected if any of my colleagues inform me otherwise, but the only evidence we have related to that are these three documents that I have shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the first document says that it had to be demolished by 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And the subsequent documents follow on in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 21st of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: They then say -- ask for the report on the action, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I will do it in redirect. It will be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We have one more document that I didn't appreciate we had. I will deal with it later, if I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So 1994, the enclave is not to survive but to disappear. Let's go to 1995, to Directive 7, which you're familiar with, you received. You received Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Can I see on the screen what it is?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: P00838. Can we have that up, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You talk about it in your statement at paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Has the witness got a copy of his statement in B/C/S? If not, I have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it could just be zoomed in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So far as the witness statement is concerned, I do have a hard copy and it might be easier for the witness to see that, if my friends don't mind. It has my markings with the exhibit number at the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can this be passed to the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can just hold on to your statement now, there is no need to refer to it quite yet. This is Directive 7. You remember it, of course. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We are going to go, please, to page 11 of the English and page 15 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just want to remind you of the language to which you've referred in your statement. And we are looking at the heading, Drina Corps, which you can see. I hope you have that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to read out the first part of the paragraph, you can see it, and it's on the record, so I'm taking it up halfway through to save time. The sentence begins: "As many enemy forces as possible should be tied down by diversionary and active combat operations," et cetera. And then it says: "While in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves." And then I'm going to ask you to -- about this sentence: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." And then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The following page in English, please, same page in B/C/S, page 11 in the English -- sorry, 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "In case the UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the DK command shall plan an operation named Jadar with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves and definitively liberating the Drina valley region."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "... create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life ..." You agree that that does not express, does it, a lawful military objective?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see here, there is a reference to the defeat of the Muslim forces, not the defeat of the Muslim people. Now, how come Muslim forces after an official signing of the cease-fire on the demilitarisation of the area? That is the substantive problem. We are not going to let them make incursions, come every now and then, kill all the inhabitants of a Serb village, et cetera, et cetera, and also to be protected by UNPROFOR forces at that. Please, do not link Muslim formations that stayed there on their own, deceiving the world. Please do not link that to the Muslim people. And it wasn't that the Muslims were only in Srebrenica. In Srebrenica there were a lot of refugees from various territories where our counteroffensive was launched as we liberated areas in Podrinje. So indeed, if the population are not in their homes, at their fields, in their barns, who is keeping them in Srebrenica? What is the objective? The answer lies there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you answer my question? "Create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa," does not express, does it, a lawful military objective?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please, what is meant here is that the existing enclaves cannot be linked up. Further on, they cannot extend to Kladanj. Further on, they cannot extend to Tuzla. That has to do with the prospect of bearability of living, not living in the enclave. I repeat, and I'm going to repeat for the 100th time, we were at war then, there was a state of war then between warring parties, but do not keep inserting the Muslim people into each and every one of your questions. Do understand that the Muslim people were never my enemy nor can they ever be my enemy. The people, I repeat, the people. But in all fairness, someone who wants to destroy the Bajina Basta hydroelectric power plant, who wants to procure weapons and ammunition to destroy half of Belgrade, those who say that I am occupying territory that is my very own village of Ratkovici, you know that the main command, Rasim Delic signed that in his own hand, you have these documents, and he says that we have temporarily occupied a territory and that's where we are. For heaven's sake, I was born there. How can I come to this temporarily occupied territory? I never said that for any particular point that the Muslims held. That it was temporarily occupied. I am pleased if that is their home, just like I'm pleased that my home is my home. But temporarily occupied territory, you're never going to find that in any one of my documents and I never allowed anyone to say anything like that in my presence either. Yet again I'm asking you, please, let us not tire ourselves out with this. Please do not drag the long-suffering people into this. Do not confuse them with the army. The army is something completely different. Especially the leadership that ignored the key document and that is the document regarding the enclaves and the demilitarisation of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's go, please -- let's go further forward in this document to English page 14 and to the B/C/S, please, page 19. We will have to go over to page -- I apologise -- page 20 in the B/C/S. And it's the second paragraph down in the B/C/S I want to read, and in the English the bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistic support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." So, General, Directive 7 requires that the starving of the Muslim population and restriction of support to UNPROFOR be unobtrusive; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do take a look at this, how much food they received, how much equipment, how much medicine, all the things they needed. They got more than they could have manufactured even in the days of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in that territory. So please take a look at this. They are saying how much goods they received and what my reaction was, vis-à-vis this population. You cannot separate me from that population. Please take a look at this. Look at the convoys that passed and when. We treated this so seriously that at brigade level, close to the enclaves, we had a liaison officer for communicating with UNPROFOR. You have reports to that effect. That's accessible to you. And this is specifically referred to, all the goods that were sent to these enclaves in order to keep life going. Food supplies were sent and also other supplies that were needed. This was a respectable quantity. There couldn't have been hungry people there. But, please, why did you not say that these same Muslim authorities abused these supplies and turned their own people into paupers, hungry paupers? I have documents to that effect, Muslims in Srebrenica. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right, they were hungry, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the truth, that is the truth. No, no. No. But they weren't hungry because of me. Again, please, don't just remember half of my sentence, remember my entire sentence. I told you look at the contingents of the supplies that arrived in the enclave. Look at the food, and look at the ratio vis-à-vis the population. I've already said that is more than they could have produced or manufactured themselves in peacetime. And I'm pleased that there was that much. The first convoy that was allowed to pass in November 1992, I stated officially that we do have a soul, that they are going to feed their children and feed their elderly, and help their frail people. What was the result? Three days later, three Serb villages were killed off in a monstrous way. And now we are talking -- oh, please, please, now we are talking about what Mother Teresa? Come on, are you telling me that the Muslim leadership did not resell these goods that was received from the world on the basis of noble decisions?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: General, your strategy was to let some convoys in, wasn't it, enough to cause a humanitarian crisis but not to expose the VRS to the condemnation of the international community that was visited upon you because of your actions under directive 4 in 1992 and 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. That is not right. Why is it not right? Which convoy was returned? In order to make you right, do tell us which convoy was returned, ever. Which convoy arrived in the area of responsibility of our units that were facing the enclave, there are reviews of impressive results there. As far as I know, not a single convoy was returned from our check-points because we would not allow them to pass through. Yes, they were kept there so that they could be checked but we never returned them, and we were always very careful so that all the goods would be kept intact and that all the people would be properly taken care of there. You have to communicate to this Court that I was even commended for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just deal with something quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have P05084? I'm just going to deal with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm afraid it is only available in English so I'm going to have to read it. It's a communication to Dr. Karadzic. Let me just read it to you. 15th of June, 1995. "We write to convoy to you our profound concern about the developing disasters in Sarajevo, Bihac, Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa due to obstructive actions by forces under your control, humanitarian supplies and relief personnel are prevented from reaching their destinations. Warehouses are empty, whole families are crying out for food, and there is little water, gas, electricity or medicine in any enclave. International humanitarian law and, indeed, human decency entitles civilians even in the midst of armed conflict to unhindered access to humanitarian supplies. The rules of international humanitarian law appear to be observed only in the breach by the Bosnian Serb military." That's right, isn't it? You observed the rules of international humanitarian law only in the breach, General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I'm answering this question once again. Which convoy was ever returned from a check-point? From a check-point of ours? Our check-points were not in Hungary or in Germany or in Holland, our check-points are 15 or 20 kilometres away from the enclave itself. Let us make a distinction there. There may have been convoys, I don't know where, but I'm talking about the convoys that reached me. Those convoys passed through. Please. There are reports to that effect. Also, there are signatures involved. There are lists that the leaders of convoys had. They were protected. It was not easy to get a convoy through such areas. Please, we all have to understand that. May this never happen again. Please don't ask me to consider these people to be my enemy. I'm going to say that for the umpteenth time. When did I ever return a convoy that reached one of my check-points? That never happened. To the best of my knowledge. And I repeat, perhaps somewhere else at a far away destination, a convoy was returned. Please don't read that out to me. Heaven forbid that any convoys were abused in any way. Those that were heading to Srebrenica, that I even took a pack of cigarettes for myself. No way. The convoys had to get through. This was our unambiguous position, and it was obvious. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: General, you tell us in paragraph 26 of your statement that Directive 7 was never implemented in practice, the tasks -- the -- I'll quote you: "The controversial portion of the directive that deals with the tasks of the Drina Corps was never implemented in practice." That's at paragraph 26, penultimate sentence. Right? Two days later, you issued an order, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could we have P3040? Dated 20 March 1995. And this is the Drina Corps command order issued pursuant to Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You recognise your order? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recognise all orders. Don't ask me if I recognise orders. If it's my order, of course I recognise it. It's not just anything. It is part of my work. How would I not recognise it if it is mine? If it is not mine, then I would not recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have page 5, please, of the English, and page 10 of the B/C/S? And we are looking under the heading, "The tasks of the Drina Corps." Forgive me, I think it's page 3 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Page -- 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we can go over in the English, please, to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we will pick it up, please, from part way through that first paragraph, this is you setting out the tasks of the Drina Corps. "In the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa. In case the UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the DK command shall plan an operation named Jadar with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves and definitively liberating the Drina valley region." So you --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, we've already discussed that. We've already answered that question about ten minutes ago. Absolutely the same words, the same text, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. You repeat the tasks assigned to the Drina Corps by Directive 7; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and what's bad about that? It's not that I made the Srebrenica or Gorazde or Zepa enclaves. They were determined by the international factor, who would be where. As for some communication, making it impossible to live in villages, Serb villages, in Zeleni Jadar, Pribojevici, Derventa, many others, these are Serb villages where they killed all their Serb neighbours, as far back as 1992, and then what? Am I supposed to build them a highway so that they can go out and do whatever they want? Do you understand that we are dealing with an enemy that is killing us and that is calling my stay in my village temporarily occupied territory. Do not forget that the latent danger that existed there day and night was the destruction of the Serb population. In the presence of the international forces. If somebody were to pass by a check-point and go back, what more can I add to that? Please find these orders where I asked UNPROFOR to withdraw these sabotage groups that freely entered the territory, to control them. They were supposed to leave their weapons and become free citizens. That's what the document about Srebrenica, Gorazde and Zepa say. It's not that they laid down their rifles. They got mortars, as a matter of fact, and they got whatever they wanted, and then they want to get me out of this temporarily occupied territory as if I did not know what land surveys were?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Making it impossible to live, make life impossible. These are words you had heard before. Let me just ask you about a meeting you attended on the 8th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have up 65 ter 21898?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When do you expect your cross-examination to be concluded, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I do apologise, Mr. President. I hadn't asked in advance for some more time. I'm afraid I got -- I lost track of the time for the last ten minutes, and I would ask for another 30 minutes, with your indulgence, Mr. President. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 30 minutes seems to be a bit too much. Could you try to conclude in 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I do apologise for not asking for more time in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: 65 ter 21898. Now, this is another of your notebooks, it's the notebook from August 1994 to 13 July 1995. You recognise the notebook, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do recognise it because it was taken away from me by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have, please, page 1 -- 111, in both B/C/S and English?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is your note of a meeting on the 8th of March, 1995, and it's at the Main Staff. Mladic is present, as are Generals Tomic, Skrbic, Colonel Beara, Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And I'd like to take you, please, to the following page, 112, this is the date, we remember, of course, that Directive 7 was issued. And you've noted down what Mladic is saying at this meeting. I'll just read a bit of it. From halfway down the page, your lines at halfway down the page, the UNPROFOR authority in Srebrenica is limited, that's Mladic. Is that what Mladic says? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it, sorry. I cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's where you have a box --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Thank you, thank you, thank you. Yes, yes, yes. I have noticed that, yes. Because we expected UNPROFOR to have the main say, not Naser Oric, and that's that. That's that. UNPROFOR is subordinated here. I wish you'd ask me more about that. UNPROFOR was subordinated here, and they had to be defended by Zivanovic. They were brought into that position. We always regarded UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me read the rest of the entry.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You told me to look. I've seen it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, it goes on. Enemy aircraft towards Srebrenica, bring down. That's Mladic. In Srebrenica details control. That's Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And on the following page, please, in the English, page 113 and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Still continuing with Mladic, make life impossible. That's what you understood to be your task, isn't it? Make life impossible for the civilian population in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Then I would prohibit the entry of convoys, then we would attack the protected enclave or fire on it, and it was strictly forbidden to fire from any sort of weapons. One of the soldiers got a son and he fired a burst of fire because he wanted to celebrate, and he was sentenced to a month in prison by me because he violated his word and my word by firing. If we had had taken this literally, make life impossible, then life would have been made impossible, but it was a far cry from that. These are flexible thoughts. It cannot be applied, because how would the army make life impossible with weapons, not with decrees but by weapons. Have I done that? No. Not in the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask for those pages, that entry of the diary, just that entry on that date, to be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with the cover page?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, please. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6483, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just, Ms. Pack or General Zivanovic, whether the general was ever investigated as a suspect or witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. From the first day, when the OTP expressed the need to meet me, I welcomed them. That was full 12 years ago. They conducted interviews with me that stretched over several days. Ms. Irene Willis and Peter McCloskey and other teams as well. We spent days and hours on end together because not for a single second did I allow myself to be unavailable to the said services. In a wish to express all my pain, the burden, the sadness, which I had lived through and experienced and saw, I simply wanted to help them with their work. For me, this is something that is elevated as a goal and as an institution, and if anyone expects salvation in all this, then it's me, because I had gone through a lot of this personally. That was why I was always available to these people, I always welcomed them properly as guests are to be welcomed, and I hope that by now they have become my friends, and I expect that from Ms. Pack as well, that everything will be fine between us as people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you ever testified before this Tribunal, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to play you a video. Could we have the first Sanction clip, please? Just before we start, this is footage from a celebration at Zvonko Bajagic's house on the 12th of July, 1995. You were celebrating the fall of Srebrenica. I'd like to play you a bit of that clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the question is?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I gather that something is wrong with the sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I don't know if you heard it. Did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I can see myself when I was younger. I can see Zvonko Bajagic, I can see one of our high priests. I see that this is in Zvonko Bajagic's house, one of the rooms of his house in Vlasenica, on the 12th of July. Please, may I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just -- just so that we know what passage we are talking about, just to refer, this is P -- from P04201, the trial video book, and I'm going to refer to the transcripts since we didn't have it orally transmitted. P04202, and I'm going to ask, please, to help us to have in e-court page 256 in English and B/C/S 355, which is the transcript from that speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm just going to read to you what was just played and you can follow in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm taking it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will not be counted as your time. While we are waiting for this transcript, General, could you tell us who was this Mr. Bajagic and what the relation with Mr. Karadzic was, as far as you understood at the time? What did he do in Vlasenica? And indeed in the Drina Corps? And what was his relation, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. First of all, it has not been said very precisely, it said celebration, and the fall of Srebrenica. We as the Orthodox Christians have our patron saint's days. The patron saint's day, or Slava in B/C/S, in Vlasenica, they exist for particular households and also for populated places. The patron saint's day of Vlasenica is the 12th of July, St. Peter's day or Petrovdan, which has been celebrated since the beginning of Christendom. That's Petrovdan, the day dedicated to St. Peter. This holiday, it's not a celebration but it's a patron saint's day so these are two different notions. A celebration is something else. It's an ad hoc events. And this is a holiday, a patron's saint's day, a religious approach to feelings we have for a saint who is believed to be a patron saint of that town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be brief in answering the question. My question was about Zvonko Bajagic, not that the -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I was about to tell you that Zvonko Bajagic, as a respected host, was the host of the celebration of this patron saint's day and the guests were invited to his private house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I was not asking about this gathering. I was -- my question was just related to Mr. Zvonko Bajagic individually, what was he, what was he doing in your Drina Corps, and what was his relationship with Mr. Karadzic. Simply that's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall answer immediately. Zvonko Bajagic was engaged in the logistics department of the Drina Corps, and I believe that he was on excellent terms both personally with Dr. Radovan Karadzic and the other members of the leadership in Pale. This is my conclusion which I drew on the basis of the insight that I had in everything that was going on at the time. So that was Zvonko Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it at that. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So the clip that was played, it's the bottom paragraph in the English. And in the B/C/S it's halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll read it: "At the beginning of June, more precisely at the end of May, we started to carry out preparations and then took Zeleni Jadar and tested what the expulsion of UNPROFOR with weapons looks like." So you're talking here, aren't you, General, about the expulsion of UNPROFOR from Zeleni Jadar, which you ordered; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was I saying this to? Who was I telling this to, please? Was it to Mladic or to Karadzic, to brigade commanders or to the priest? I was conversing with the priest and this is an abuse of this story. I'm not going to say before a priest that I paid the UNPROFOR members to move. This was a simple conversation between me, as the ex-commander already because I was many kilometres away from Srebrenica. On the 11th of July, Srebrenica was included in the Serbian territory. This was the 12th of July. I was in Vlasenica in a private visit at Zvonko Bajagic's house and talking with the priest, who was very much interested to hear what happened with the church in Srebrenica. So that was the point of the whole story.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we should play the tape. Unfortunately what's happened, as I understand, there is something wrong with the sound and -- which hasn't been resolved quite yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I don't understand, Mr. Zivanovic, that this is an abuse of this story. Did you mean that you lied to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There is no lying. It wasn't lying, nor was it an official report or debriefing. It was just a conversation between me and the Orthodox priest. It's not an official report to anyone, to my superiors or those who were my equals or those who were my subordinates. It was a conversation. I could have told the priest this differently because the priest was a person who did not take any part in combat activities. There was no reason. I mean, why? This would have no impact on -- what we told each other would not have an impact on anyone, what I told the priest and what he replied to me. So I was not directing my subordinates or sending false reports to my superiors, God forbid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please listen to the question carefully. The question was whether it was an official -- a report or a private conversation. Yes, irrespective whether it's official or private, the question was whether the content is true. So you do not deny having said these kinds of word at that gathering on the St. Peter's day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm not denying. It's the truth. What is there to deny? Of course, I'm not denying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Back to you, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps then I don't need to play the tape. Let me just go on to another portion of the transcript, if I may. So we'll go on to page 257 of the English, B/C/S, please, page 355 and we will quickly go on to 356.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is still your speech, again about Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it, I'm sorry, but I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Bottom of the page in B/C/S, bottom of the page in B/C/S, please, and it's from the paragraph, "However, we knew," in English. Let me start reading the bottom of the page in the B/C/S -- sorry, it's page 355 in the B/C/S and it's the bottom of the page. I think there might be -- there is one last sentence there that you -- you can't see, it just needs to be scrolled down a bit. There we go. Thank you. So we are going to go quickly over in the B/C/S to the following page. "However, we knew that the main strike would be on the already-built asphalt road Jadar-Srebrenica as was done, our forces physically and mentally well prepared, thank heaven, this also emotionally matured in the Serbian soldiers, the commanders not regretting any effort, the Chief of Staff, you know very well that the man is practically without one leg." That's Krstic. "But he was in the field non-stop. And that upon permission of the Main Staff commander, we established a forward command post, organised a capable command and were ready to carry out what we attempted with forceful strikes of the army. Taking into account every single soldier and the smallest of his fingers, we managed in a short time to take the dominant facilities, putting the liberation of Srebrenica at risk."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So there you are, when celebrating the victory on the 12th of July, you were saying clearly that the early attack on Zeleni Jadar, preparations for which were started in May, that was a test, and that you already knew that the attack on Srebrenica would come from the Jadar road; right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Srebrenica was never prepared or designed in my mind. That can be confirmed, and it's recorded in a thousand places, that I strictly forbid my subordinate officers and my own command to attack Srebrenica. However, I did advocate, and I stand by that to this day, that the Jadar valley, which separates the Zepa territory from the territory of Srebrenica, roughly speaking, separates or divides them, that it should officially be under our control, all of it, because that would prevent the two enclaves from linking up, and that's true. So if we held those facilities, which as a soldier I had to know, then with few forces, we could survive in such -- in this area and on those features, but there was some work in order to take hold of them. When we took hold of the dominant features, on the 10th of July, a Muslim killed a Dutch soldier from a six-metre distance. I'm a ballistics expert by profession, so on 10 July at 10.00 a.m. from six-metres distance. Why? Because he believed that this UNPROFOR APC and the UNPROFOR soldiers were his reconnaissance men, and this is incontrovertible. That's what it is. And that's my answer to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, we haven't much time so I'm going to take you to two further sections of this speech --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. General, you do not deny having said that, again? This is your words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. But just to be clear, that dominant features are to be held, which would not allow the military contingents from Srebrenica and Zepa to link up. That was my natural response to their planned offensive. So I ask you to see a document that says how much new ammunition the 28th Division from Srebrenica was asking for. So please, I beg you, have a look at that document. What was I supposed to do, to allow them to hold the vital features, in military terms, to allow them to hold them? Was I supposed to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can go on to the end of this session, if necessary, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wondered if I could ask if we could perhaps take the break earlier so that we could resolve the situation of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And it will be so much quicker, in my submission, if I can just play the General the video and then I won't have to go through the individual portions of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you for the early adjournment. The video issue has been resolved. And if I can have that played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Going on the road to Srebrenica, I saw the most Turkish mosques that one can imagine and I guess that those enemies of ours wanted it to be higher than the church, and therefore they took down half of the belfry to make the minaret a bit higher. However, they asked me this morning, General, has this famous mosque been finished? I told them I think that they finished it, so I said that it was finished this morning. And further on" --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just pausing at 00.40.31.6.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're talking about one of the mosques in Srebrenica there, are you? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We can go on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The town as such was not crowded as you can hear on the radios, no, no it was not like that. They had fantastic weaponry and Motorolas and scared, gullible units. It is best to listen to the Turks as little as possible and one should not listen to some Serbs either. Take a sword in your hands. Our forces came towards Potocari. The police forces were introduced from Bratunac. One wing of our army went towards Viogor. Viogor is the crest of the hill towards Milici and Srebrenica and so, God willing, we will get to Derventa from Srebrenica. This is our task. And yesterday with the fall of -- not from Milici to Derventa, from Srebrenica to Derventa. Yes, from Srebrenica to Derventa. Let me tell you that with yesterday's dusk, any organised Muslim life to the left of Jadar ceased existing. Meaning nothing of Kutuzero, nothing of Bucje, nothing of this old story, all of it is over. They left their cannons, rifles. And really, yesterday in Srebrenica I saw cooked beans but no household. The pie is hot but nobody left to eat it. That means they were there just very, very recently. And here we come."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's at 00.42.10.1. That last extract is at page 259 of the English e-court, P04202. So, General Zivanovic, any organised life, Muslim life to the left of Jadar ceased existing. This is similar, isn't it, to the language of Directive 7, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants, the inhabitants, not the enemy, of Srebrenica and Zepa. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. And why not? Because all the population was moved away from the line between the units. I mentioned the left bank of the Jadar. The dominant features with military views show that whoever holds these features would either join up or separate the enclaves. As this was the area where the Serbian army had already entered, to my happiness, then and now, the population was not affected by the combat. It moved to Susnjari and Milacevici area and no one fired at this area with anything. We could have fired with rifles and cannons but we didn't because the population was there. And that's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm at the end of my time. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me begin with the freshest points. Can you tell us about the circumstances concerning the mosque? What did you mean? Why was the mosque destroyed or shortened? What was this talk about the church and the mosque? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica had four mosques and one Orthodox Church in town, and one Orthodox Church between Srebrenica and Potocari, at the Orthodox Serbian cemetery of Srebrenica. From the positions that we held around the enclave, Srebrenica, of course, was visible, and we saw, even before we entered Srebrenica, I mean the scouts saw that the cross was taken off the church, the bells were taken down, and the tower was cut in half. When I talked to the people who were very pained over this, they said it will be destroyed completely. I said no, it won't be. Why? When this church was designed -- because I consider Srebrenica as my own town, that's where I grew up, that's where I finished high school, I was president of my class, I spread literacy among young people, both Serbs and Muslims, I participated in the foresting effort, quite simply I love Srebrenica. I have many, many friends there. And when this new mosque was supposed to be built, with a very big, big minaret, there was a lot of debate when they were making models for the mosque. Their desire was to make the minaret higher than the cross, but since I am a topographer I know about altitudinal differences. So willy-nilly, the mosque had to be lower than the church because it was laid on lower ground. If they had wanted out of some rivalry to make it higher, they should have put it atop a hill. So what happened? When we entered Srebrenica, around 5.00 p.m., on the 11th of July, in the portal of the church, I saw, and not only I but anybody who was willing to look, I saw Muslim cattle coming out of the barn. I went up to the church and I saw a horrific sight. The bells were on the ground by the entrance. The ropes from the bells were tied to the cattle, to keep them on a leash. It was very humiliating. And when I talked to the priest, and you showed a bit of this conversation, I can't remember anymore what we said to each other, anyway, I talked to this priest, Kacavenda, and I told him: Just clean up, never mind the ropes and the cattle, just don't let them turn our church into a barn, as they did. Every soldier had to be distressed when he saw that sight, and I knew very well that they would destroy the mosque and there was no chance of preventing them after they saw the church the way it looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone issue orders to destroy the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no order, especially since I returned from Srebrenica on the 11th, and as the whole world knows and the Office of the Prosecutor, to whom I gave extensive statements, I was no longer engaged in that area. You saw from the recording that I was in Vlasenica. Later -- and Vlasenica is 50 kilometres away from Srebrenica. I was away when all this was going on. But even a lay person would expect that mosque to be destroyed in view of what had happened to the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Drina Corps and the VRS in general deal with civilian aspects of life, the right of civilians to return? Whose job was it in the system of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was within the purview of the authorities. Yesterday, and earlier today, attempts were made to pretend that I was some sort of commissioner for either the Serbs or the Muslims. You know, as the accused here, that you were at the top of our government. We had a regulated political governmental life at the level of municipalities, and public utilities were in operation, schools were in operation, hospitals as well. Everything was functioning. And I have to tell you this as well: We did everything so that the school in Srebrenica could continue working. Not a single shell fell in its vicinity. Why doesn't the world hear more about that? We were only waiting patiently for demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you, General. What does the army mean when they say that you should abolish enclaves? Does that refer to civilian life or to military aspects? What was the attitude of the Drina Corps, and what would it have been if the enclaves had really been demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret to this day that peace did not come on that day, because of all the supplies that were requested by Srebrenica, they never requested a single agricultural machine, any tools necessary for work in the factory. They didn't ask for anything that was necessary to revive economic life. Look at the last paragraph in the order that came from your level about demilitarisation. I believe it was the 23rd or the 24th of March, 1994. It says in the last paragraph that Muslim soldiers who had laid down their arms become civilians and free citizens, and that was an opportunity, a chance, and it also says that they have the right to free movement. If that had happened, the corps would not have any role with regard to them anymore. Every demobed soldier has the right to go home, the way it happens today. Nobody would have prevented a man who used to be a soldier in Srebrenica from going home. That was the firm position, and I'm full of regret to this day that demilitarisation never happened, and I'm not sure that the places of deployment for UNPROFOR were the best possible solution. They should have said, "Muslims go 500 metres back, Serbs go 500 metres back. The politicians should now come and deal with the situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When the term "mopping up" a certain area is used in the army, or clearing a certain area, my learned friend added to this term, ethnic cleansing. Could you tell me what the army means, clearing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means clearing from enemy troops and weapons, so that our personnel be safe. But the opposing party did not accept that for a moment. They destroyed and stole all my property. To this day, nobody apologised to me, nobody said, "I'm sorry."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document 04075 be shown to the witness, document on the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 89, it was suggested that we wanted -- or, rather, that Mladic said on that occasion that Muslims should disappear from that area. Could we please look at that document? Did the army have any plans to prevent civilians from returning to their homes after the fighting was over?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never wanted that. I, as a commander, always wanted everyone to come back to their home. Yesterday, I tried to give a more extensive answer to that question but, unfortunately, Madam Prosecutor cut me off. When Skelani fell, as the last point, that was the 17th of January, 1993, where they had killed students and teachers together, where they had caused a lot of suffering and pain and death, I'm saying this not because I'm your witness here, but I, without you knowing or Mladic knowing, I established a direct line with the Muslim side, knowing that you would approve. I didn't allow Naser Oric to come. I wanted people of some sobriety to come, such as the hodza from Srebrenica. I wanted to invite people of that kind, to discuss what we should do. Our basic task was - it could be a harsh sentence to me - and that was that Muslims, and that was before the offensive started, they had before that burned down Serb villages, I, myself, came into a Serbian village that had been destroyed and collected mortal remains of some bodies and got them autopsied later by Dr. Stankovic from the military medical academy. So our position was that they should stay at home and work on their farms, on their estates, and leave politics to others, and I would invest my own authority, telling them that they would be safe if they stayed at home. And these peasants, if they had stayed in their homes as free citizens, then my own refugees would come back to their villages more easily. I have 50 photos where you can see me working together with these people after, to rebuild my own house that Naser Oric had razed to the ground, whereas I had spared his own house. Unfortunately nobody listened to me. Do you know what answer I received from the Muslim side? That they were stronger. And what came later? The counteroffensive, and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you see the second paragraph in point 1, where it refers to the cutting of trees and undergrowth. Is it a defensive or offensive action?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a classic part of defensive activities. You see, one word here changes all the meaning. Cut through. That means cut down the growth and the trees to enable visibility, observation. To cut off, on the other hand, means to disable a certain communication, to prevent it from being used, whereas cutting through, that means cleaning the undergrowth, just as is normally done, because in -- in the woods, you can't see anything from the trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber whether setting mines before one's forward line is a defensive or an offensive action?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cutting through, as the first defence action, makes way for fire protection, and what is important about setting these mines? It's important to set them according to the solutions decided by the commander, and these mines must be protected. There must be strict protocols and records so that later on, when these mines are no longer needed, they could be efficiently and easily removed. I'll give you a very graphic example. A girl found herself in a minefield, running from the Srebrenica units. This girl, this Muslim girl, of course, was saved thanks to the fact that I was close. We managed to get her out of the minefield and we took her -- and believe me, the priest was not so pleased with me, because I knew his car was very good and had enough fuel. I told the medical people: Put the girl in the priest's car. We took her to Uzice and I even found the time to go and visit her. Why? Because she was the daughter of Zulfo Tursunovic, who, in 1984, killed her father by cutting his throat. These are very complex life stories. It was very complex work. And of course, the girl was very grateful to me later for saving her life and for bringing her to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You now just confirmed that you did not foster any ideas about a permanent removal of the Muslim population from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way, not for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page, please. This was discussed yesterday at page 89 of the transcript. Now I'm going to read this out. It's the last paragraph under number 2. So it's the subparagraph before paragraph 3: The life of the enemy has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave should be made impossible --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is meant when it says "enemy" and "temporarily"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant is the armed force that abused, did not honour the agreements on demilitarisation. Believe me, I am so sorry, and it pains me to think that these people there were used as a mask, and then when day-time comes, then they say good morning. To this day Muslims call me to build houses with them together. I don't know, but they keep inviting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you mentioned that Srebrenica was full of people from other municipalities, and then the Prosecutor suggested to you that we had expelled these people. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where, during which operation, the Army of Republika Srpska came into physical contact with civilians and affected their behaviour? How did that happen? Where were the civilians and where was the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is the truth. And may all survivors say, whether they were in civilian activities and whether I was involved in military activities, civilians were always taken behind the lines, and we clashed with a division, a division is quite big. There are military rules involved. That's the way it is. In America, France, China, wherever. However, this is the essence. If you will believe me, we really did our very best to spare civilians in combat operations. Please, nobody asked me what I saw. As for the population, as for Srebrenica, if you'll allow me to say just for one minute, when we went from Pribicevac, from the command post there, I did -- my driver did not go with me. The -- my escort was driving, it was only three of us, my brother, I and the driver, when we came to Kvarc trig 3.013 metres, it's the most important feature there, from Kvarc you can see clearly from Jadar to Bratunac, and the part of Srebrenica that leads to Solotis [phoen] and Potocari is particularly visible, to Milacevici, Ravni Buljim, et cetera. Now, Susnjari, Milacevici, Lokotosa [phoen], so it's a Serb village, it was emptied already in the beginning of May 1992, totally destroyed, not to mention Susnjari, that it was even earlier on, and we saw with our very own eyes, columns, columns of civilians, soldiers, men, women, who were marching along those roads. You could fire any which way you wanted at such columns. However, I claim with full responsibility, and thank God this has been proven by time, no one dared fire at these columns and no one did fire at these columns. That's how Srebrenica was emptied, emptied, and soldiers entered Srebrenica without any combat involved, as far as Srebrenica is concerned. Some people were even teasing me, they were saying how could I as a professor from the military academy, for 12 years I was a professor, a professor of ballistics, how come I'm not firing at the road but this way or that way. But my order was -- and nobody keeps showing these orders. My orders were that I banned any kind of fire at any formations that were not part of the combat disposition. So especially because there were civilians there, men, women, there was a mix of people there, and they managed to leave unhindered. While I was in that area, Srebrenica was not torched, all the inhabitants of that municipality left, I went further on and I know as much as you do. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, were you at your command post when civilians, in 1993, from Cerska, Kamenica and all the other villages, set out to Srebrenica? Were these columns visible to you and how many times was fire opened at these columns?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to answer your question about the atrocities committed in Serb villages -- sorry, did you hear what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm reading, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat. First I have to talk about the atrocities in the Serb villages between Vlasenica and Cerska in 1992. It's not one village. All the Serb villages were destroyed and everybody was killed. And such atrocities were committed, such crimes were committed, that people who do not have a good stomach or a good nervous system should not look at those photographs. It is terrible. Now, since this Cerska was indeed quite a stronghold, I have to remind you that we were warring parties, it's not that we were involved in farming work together. We set -- they set out towards Srebrenica and they had these points of resistance, Koglici [phoen], and these other points where you can defend it. As you enter the valley of Konjevic Polje, there was no fighting. Yesterday, we saw that Pandurevic said that it should not be destroyed, torched, and there were people who were homeless. So these columns mainly went towards Srebrenica. Now, I have information because a Muslim came to see me in Vlasenica, and he beseeched me not to allow -- how did he put this? Well, let me put it this way: That I should not allow suspicious individuals to be in positions of authority. The man came to see me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You, your troops, could you see this column of civilians? Actually, first of all, did your troops have physical contact with civilians from Kamenica, Cerska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with civilians, exceptionally those who slaughtered those Serb villages, with them, yes. And civilians of course left. I have to tell you this. The terrain is such, it is so hard to have combat in areas like that, and especially to be on the move, the enemy can suffer terrible losses in such terrain, but I keep repeating that it was not my aim to have people killed. These poor people did not have enough to eat and they did not have the right kind of clothing but then I could not help anyone with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember in the world media and in UNPROFOR what was stated about what our army did vis-à-vis the civilians in Cerska in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you something else. This is an entire conglomerate, has to do with news, and it's hard to say everything in one answer. Actually, these reports were not only unfavourable but they were unsincere because nobody really wanted to muddy their boots and go out into the terrain and see what the situation was like. They received reports from one office to another, and really, on the ground itself, well, very few people got to the right information there. And people say somebody called me from Zvornik on the 12th or on the 13th and some officer of theirs called me and said, There are 5.000 Turks, even more people -- more than the inhabitants of Zvornik. And I said, Who said that to you? And he said, The colleague from the office next door. And I said, Well, just tell him to forget it. So we cannot just take things at face value. So this was the time when people were trying to brag in newspapers and make these bombastic statements, but hardly anyone got to the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether General Morillon visited Cerska to see for himself, as you said, put on his own boots and go out and see what is happening, and were the allegations concerning the massacre correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean massacre? I asked this same Morillon, I beseeched him, well, Hayes is still alive, let him say, and I wanted them to say -- well, I told them let people live. Forget about this silly business of yours. People were so indoctrinated and it was hard to think in normal terms, in terms of normal life. Well, let me tell you, Morillon had to be -- how do I put this? He had to be far more diligent if he had this kind of statesmanly responsibility. He should have been a lot more vigilant but he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You were asked about convoys yesterday, the difficulties involved and the reasons. So there was resistance among the Serb population, but sometimes, in some areas, were there military reasons for postponing convoys, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And why? Because in convoys there were goods that did not match the lists provided. There were even weapons there. I was never at a check-point myself so I didn't do the counting. But there was this kind of abuse. Please, I'm not saying that somebody had planned this, somebody who wanted to cheat with the convoys. So even those people who wanted to help sincerely were cheated because things were sent through these convoys that were not really supposed to assist the population. Sorry, I mean if they are sending rifles, then it's different. I'm a soldier, I have to put it that way. Do not fill a sack with ammunition and say that you're taking that sack to feed the children. How can anyone even think of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I really meant was whether there were any military developments involved? Did the convoys have to go through the front line itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you do when there was fighting on the ground where the convoy was supposed to pass?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times, the convoy would be checked and then it would move on. However, what happened? The front part of the convoy would already enter the area where there was combat. Oh, please, please. Combat was already underway. So what? Stop convoys? Stop, stop? So it's not that they were stopped for just any old reason. They were stopped because there was fighting going on. So until you created conditions for seeing which way people were going, I mean how could I know whose intentions were whatever? If a convoy was allowed to go towards Srebrenica, then quite simply they had to get there safely. Truth to tell, it's better for them to wait for a certain period of time and for the convoy to arrive so that no one would get killed from that convoy, heaven forbid. I would consider that to be a terrible defeat of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that we are going to get to documents of this nature if we have enough time. However, I would like to dwell on the claims made by the Prosecution today. It was alleged that the Drina Corps had the task of causing a humanitarian disaster by restricting humanitarian aid and weakening the military power of UNPROFOR by imposing restrictions on them. First of all, tell us, the entire population of the municipality of Srebrenica, did all of them live in the small town of Srebrenica itself or, rather, did they live in villages and was there a rural production there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they refused my offer, in 1993, to hand over weapons and to remain as free citizens in their own households, when they responded that they were stronger, of course we launched a counteroffensive and there were organised Muslim formations facing us. The population kept withdrawing, retreating, and they got into an area, the municipal centre of Srebrenica, and I personally did the measuring, 5 kilometres by 1 and a half kilometres, and there is nothing in Srebrenica except for houses and the municipality. The very entering of the population into Srebrenica that way is quite a problem. I know each and every part of Srebrenica. I used to live there as a tenant in Muslim families, Serb families. So this was a bad idea. And, sir, there was no production, not any rural production. Srebrenica does not have a single hectare of arable land. Let us look at each and every plot of land there on the basis of the land register, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about UNPROFOR? Did they have drills or exercises, target practice? Did UNPROFOR ask for fresh ammunition supplies, and if so, where could they use this ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I secured UNPROFOR movements. I was their rifle and ammunition for as long as they were in my territory, if I can put it that way. When I said "my territory," I meant where I was commander and where my units were present. There were no weapons that were needed, no rifles, no nothing, as I've already said. Their main rifle was their UNPROFOR insignia on their sleeves and their blue helmets. Those were their weapons.
