There would be one observation post and then seven kilometres away there would be another one. I don't even know whether they had radio communication, let alone any other kind of communication. So it's not that they had any kind of target practice or whatever. There weren't any training grounds there at all. After all, we communicated with them, socialised with them. Let many of these UNPROFOR people say how much time they spent with me, and had proper inter-human relationships. Now, whether somebody abused this and whether they gave the military formations of the Muslims ammunition, well, you have to ask them or, rather, they have to ask themselves, not me. Because no one ever told me or announced that there would be military exercises of UNPROFOR carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D3313, could we briefly take a look that in e-court? This is a Muslim document. The state security sector from Tuzla. That's not the document. Could we then, please, have a look at 1D29081?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, this is Prijedor. It's not the Drina area. Drina and Prijedor are not together.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D92081, then, please. This is it. Let's have a look. First, the document dated the 23rd of November, 1995, the state security sector Tuzla. Can we please look at page 10, first? I'm sorry that it's not translated but I didn't know that that would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please focus on what it says here, the overview of available information about murders, criminal activities, prostitution and other committed in the area of Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Going into the detail, given that we do not have English translation, please let us know what this document is about, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see. I can't see it. I'm sorry, I apologise, I can't see anything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in and can you read out for us what the subject of the document is? It's up here. Whose document is this? Can we show the heading, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go to the first page, first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a set of documents, Your Excellency, and this document is independent. It's a set of documents under the same number but this document has its own heading and its own date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then go back to the page you want to show us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, if we can zoom in on to the heading first, would you agree with me that it comes from the state security in Tuzla, the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see, unfortunately. It's not marked. Yes, that's right, correct. Their security service of their corps command. It's their document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it say about the subject? What's the subject?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overview of available information about committed murders, criminal activities, prostitution, et cetera, in the area of Srebrenica in the period up until the occupation of this protected zone. This is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. I really don't see how this comes out of my cross, a document about whatever topics this is that I can't read. But just from the summary, I don't see how this arises out of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just identifying the document and on page 15 is what follows from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having viewed this title, could you assist us how this arises out of the line of cross-examination of Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, in the cross-examination it was claimed that the Drina Corps restricted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we hear that in the absence of the witness? Or could you tell us in English briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you kindly take off your headset for the moment? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellency, since this title hadn't been read and translated entirely, it is about the criminal activities in Srebrenica and it is concerning humanitarian aid, abuse, stealing and trading humanitarian aid with a lot of -- lot of those aid -- this aid that was on the black market.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is it related to Ms. Pack's cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellency, Prosecution alleged that General Zivanovic and Drina Corps restricted flow of humanitarian aid in Srebrenica, while General Zivanovic said that they did have enough, they abused it, they used to sell it, and so on. And this Muslim document is exactly talking about that. So all of our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. We will allow the question. Yes, please, yes, I'll use the body language. He understood.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the paragraph, the 7th from above, which says from humanitarian aid, a large quantity of goods were set aside for the needs of the 28th Division, of which a significant part intended for Oric were sold at the market by Hamdija Fejzic, Suljo Konakovic, Amer Mehmedovic and so on. Did you know this and how does this fit with your knowledge about the situation with regard to food and the destiny of the humanitarian aid which you let pass through?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This confirms my evidence and proves that the humanitarian aid which was transferred to Srebrenica was improperly distributed, because it wasn't given out to the homeless people and refugees, to them primarily, to children and everyone else, but, as the document itself says, even Naser's market was functional. They sold the same goods there. So there were not only 20 or 50 Muslims who were armed so that you couldn't see them. The formations were somewhat stronger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you want to say that the 28th Division, the food for them, that they were giving humanitarian aid to their army? Wasn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was how they kept their army. It was fine for the army. They had everything. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we just be as brief as possible, General? Could we look at item 2, lower down - if we can scroll up - Hasanovic Suljo, the former chief of the Secretariat of People's Defence in Srebrenica took food and food items from the humanitarian aid depot, sold one part of it at the market, by using unidentified persons, and he used to make his own brandy by using some of the food items. How does that fit into your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the abuse of humanitarian aid, and we turned everyone's attention of that in November 1992. You should look at my statement which I said after the first convoy passed through, when I was removing Serbian women who were dressed in black from the road so that the convoy could pass through, I had to discuss this with the soldiers, I had to move the rifles aside, as bullrush so that the convoy could pass through. So I exposed myself to some risks, and it's unjust that this should be minimised, so what would happen? Three or four new Serbian villages would cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you connect the passage of humanitarian aid with subsequent torching of Serbian villages that occurred soon after this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what any normal man would find despicable and astonishing. You help someone and he returns by firing and using rifles. I told you, I sent you a document, saying that such conduct -- we acted in a cosmopolitan way. The aid has to pass through, the people are threatened because those were our neighbours, we grew up with them, we went to school with them, we built houses with them, we created everything with them, we fought with them, we learned together with them, and now suddenly there were some people, let me call them men, who turned everything upside down. I made my house in Ratkovici together with Muslims with a wish to grow old together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the next page, now? Item 5 at the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here, Dr. Avdo Hasanovic, the head of the war hospital in Srebrenica, medication at the hospital was sent at the price of 100 to 200 Deutschmarks which caused the deaths of many people, mainly the soldiers of the BH Army. If you had said this rather than having your document from the Muslim secret service, would you be believed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be a perjurer officially and probably also a fool, if you will excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As if I didn't know what they were doing. Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 7, Zulfo Tursunovic, former commander of -- former brigade commander in the 28th Division. From the depot containing humanitarian aid, goods, the members of the command staff of the 28th Division could take away significant quantities of goods. Tursunovic did not need an approval to be allowed to enter the depot, whenever he visited the depot, the goods were issued to him regardless of what he requested and how much. A little bit down, under item 9, it says that this one Mehoric had a batch of horses and that he fed them with wheat and sugar at the time of the greatest want. And that he was organising the reselling of humanitarian goods through a racketeer called Sirhan, who is currently in the free territory. Did you know how the humanitarian aid was used?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew personally the men whose names you've listed, the one who is called Mehoric, who had his horses, that was in the Luka village, close to village -- Luka and Krusev Do belong to Srebrenica, the Srebrenica municipality even though they are far away from Srebrenica, eight hours on foot. That was why some honourable men, the Muslims, requested from me -- but the enemy side called me to be their commander because they said, The people on our side have stolen everything and the people have gone to the dogs. So if you'll allow me I told them, Look, this is ridiculous, how can I be a commander to one side until noon and then the commander of the other side from noon onwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. On the occasion of the directive number 7, the Prosecution made the claim that the Drina Corps and you personally starved the people by restricting the passage of humanitarian aid convoys. I would like to show you now two documents, one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we could show D3947 on one part of the screen, that's the overview of the delivered humanitarian aid that was delivered to the enclaves in 1994, and on the other part of the screen, 1D5406. No translation, but we'll manage. For 1995, immediately after directive 7. Could we also admit the previous document to have it MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Marked for identification but not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI D3956, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, only those two pages. We will admit only those two pages shown to the witness. I meant marking it for identification. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid, Your Excellency, that I have shown more than two. We had page 10, page 15, page 16, and page 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should stand corrected. Yes, those four pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, please help us. If necessary, we can lower the upper document so that we can see that it refers to 1994. Can you read out --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can see it. The upper one. I see it. As you see, the first 14 items are in tonnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Can you please read for us the titles of the one that's up and down?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overview of humanitarian aid delivered to the Srebrenica enclave in 1994. Each kilo, each item here is noted by our officers, liaison officers in charge of contact with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Can we just be as focused as possible so that we would spend as little time as possible. So up there, in 1994, can you please slowly read out the title of the lower document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you slow down both of you and put a pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see how this newly arises out of my cross-examination because it's dealt with in the witness statement. This is what -- why he was cross-examined on the topic because he gave evidence in his witness statement, not least at paragraph 26 and then again in the addendum, the new bit, on the topic of humanitarian aid. It's been addressed in direct and, in my submission, doesn't arise from my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me see the title of the document that was not dealt with in his statement? Could you read the title again, please? Lower one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lower one, survey of humanitarian aid to Muslim enclaves for March and April 1995. The unit of measurement is again tonne, and you can see the breakdown by month and quantity. These amounts of food, looking at the number of the population, and the capacities of production before the war, the production could not provide these quantities of food. I say this with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll allow you -- I'm sorry, the Chamber will allow you to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, is it correct - I'm talking about the upper document - that flour was delivered, 216 tonnes in October 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the upper document was already admitted, but when you start your question with "is it correct," that always has been leading. Bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How much flour -- look at line 1 for 1994. How much flour was delivered in October, November and December 1994? And how much in March and April 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see in item 1: Month of October, 216; November, 271 tonnes; and December, when we had snow and winter, 1262 tonnes. A total of 5051 tonnes. That is an impressive figure that certainly means nobody went hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at how much flour was delivered in March and how much in April, to Srebrenica. Let's leave Gorazde aside. Just Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March, 305 tonnes. And in April, 387 tonnes. And you see the totals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After the 8th of March, and after the issuing of directive 7, did your corps restrict and reduce deliveries of flour to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we see here, not by one kilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at how many beans came into Srebrenica in October through December and in March and April. Tonnes of beans?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: October, 11; November, 12.1 tonnes; December, 1 tonne. Total 381 tonnes. That's more than the entire Eastern Bosnia could produce. In March 1995, for Srebrenica, 36 tonnes; April, 44. If these were beans grown in Srebrenica, what joy it would have been. But it couldn't have been grown in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were some items considerably reduced, in the lower document compared to the upper document, in the last three months of 1994 and the first months of 1995 after the issuing of the directive? Look at indicators for sugar?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Enough was provided so that people could decently live. But I have to say that when Muslims reported their numbers, these numbers could only be explained by a double birth rate than they really had. But we always tried to provide as much as we could, especially for the people who were -- the poor people inside Srebrenica itself. Of course, most of the Serbs had been expelled from Srebrenica long before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be MFIed pending translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D3957.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, today on page 2, when you were asked about the water-tower, you said that the water-tower was almost in ruins already when the order was given to destroy it, and you said that it was destroyed because it had been serving a military purpose. Can you remember on what date Mr. Skocajic wrote that letter where he interprets your words and on what date was the first demolishing of the tower?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's say it's March [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can answer the main point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? The tower --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 23, I didn't mention March. I said let's call up the document, the one written by Mr. Skocajic. P05148, I believe. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we make this larger? It's too small to read. 31st of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look again now at P5149, your document. The document is dated 21st of June. Please look at the first paragraph, discussing the day when this water-tower was damaged. Which date do we see in the first paragraph concerning the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26th of May, that's before the order to destroy the tower. It's simply unbelievable the troubles we faced. This combat action took place before, and this tower served no other purpose but for observers to make sure that nobody approach or damage the water supply. And now people are saying that I cut off water to the Muslims, whereas I brought Koljevic himself into inspection. Muslim people have never been my enemies. Let's make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just confirm what came first?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First there was a sabotage against the water supply section that was in the vicinity of the UN check-point. They passed by past the check-point, damaged the water supply, and then they started using the water-tower for military purposes, as an observation point, and that's when I said let's put a stop to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you know about my position concerning the use of water supply and other utilities for military purposes? That is concerning the abuse of such installations.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say very sincerely here or anywhere else, your position concerning the preservation of economic resources and human resources and reducing tensions between the warring parties was of inestimable value. There is no dilemma about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just show D104 to the General for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you go on, I would like the witness to read out this document in its entirety. Do you remember this document, General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can collapse the English for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of course. This was sent by Colonel Vukota Vukovic, who was one of the commanders subordinated to me, who was in that area with the primary task of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just I would like you to read out the contents of the document first and then I will ask you a question. If you remember the content of this document, then I will put the question right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the essence of this document, yes. You can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's talking about the Muslim attack on the 26th, and -- correct, General? And the protest made on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. That's right, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what was the date of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 21st of June, 1993, at 1715 hours, written by Vukota Vukotic. On the 26th of May at 2058 hours, a Muslim sabotage group made an incursion into the area with a clear objective of carrying out a sabotage action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question to you, General, is that if the attack was on 26th of May, and the protest to the UNPROFOR was made on the 27th of May, why is this Colonel Vukovic making his report to the -- to you a month later, i.e. on the 21st of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sorry, Your Excellency, it was not a month later. It must be a mistake. About such things we communicated within the same day. It would have been completely useless to report it so much later because there were wounded. There had been an armed clash. I needed to know immediately. It must have been some sort of mistake. As for the functioning of reporting, we were always receiving reports in a timely manner and I immediately reported upwards to my superiors. Such incidents had to be notified to the superior command as well. It must have been a mistake in the date, but that's the essence of the document. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If such incident had taken place, it should have been reported immediately following the events? That's what you just said now, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can we go back to the previous document, P5147?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if I may be of assistance you should ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have ample opportunity. This document -- we can collapse the English so that the witness can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is an order from Skocajic to demolish the water-tower by 1st of June, and it also says it should be presented to the public to have been done by Muslims, and it was dated 31st of May. So having -- having seen the document, one may view that the last -- the previous document we saw by Vukovic, Vukota Vukovic, was a fake one to present that it was -- it had been done by the Muslims. What do you -- what is your observation? Do you have anything to say to such observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have to tell the truth, and that is: This is not a triangle, Skocajic, Vukovic, Zivanovic, this is, rather, Vukovic's conversation and the protest he made to the UN personnel who made a record and that is proof of the truthfulness of these events because people are named here, the exact location, and the reaction of the UNPROFOR commander. About the dates, this confusion about the dates, the transmitter where Vukota was is located in the mountains and it was powered by a generator. It could have malfunctioned, but the action itself is crystal clear because he really made a submission with the UNPROFOR command and reported up to us what was going on. I see the decision in the UNPROFOR document which was drafted, and it proves every word I said, because my subordinates did not dare deceive me. I was not a man who sat in his office and just took people's word for it. I -- although I was very seriously wounded and in pain, I constantly moved around and inspected positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, when a regular combat report is sent to you, is it sent on the same day? Do you request it by writing your own dispatch or is it sent to you automatically?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in peacetime, when we, military personnel, are not involved in a war, there is a perfectly regulated system of reporting based on subordination. Of course, the superior command does not need to request a report because the subordinate command knows exactly what they have to report on, item by item, and if there is no change in a certain area, they just write, "No change." But they know perfectly well that the superior command has to be notified about the situation in the subordinate unit. If, however, a sudden change occurs, such as an assault of enemy forces against our positions, then an interim report is sent immediately, immediately, and the superior command will have to decide then whether to accept engagement with the available forces or they will make an alternative decision, whatever is best. I remember there was a similar question from those who interrogated me a few years ago or, rather, ten years ago, they asked me about a similar document, who signed it, and it so happened that it was Krstic who signed his report for the 13th --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to ask you: Did the superior command ask -- does a superior command ask for an interim report or is it sent automatically?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is sent automatically, in particular because if a problem can escalate, then things have to be dealt with urgently, even by the command above that one, even the president, you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in which situations the higher command asks by way of a dispatch for a report subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To see whether something had been done, what is new, what is not new, and it is -- and what is important for the level of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we return the previous document on the screen, please? The previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I'm trying to finish before the break so that we don't keep you longer and that's why I'm hoping for shorter answers. Can we zoom in on the upper part, General, sir, can you tell us what this means? Your dispatch related to your dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember what was requested by this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. To see what happened, to receive a report what happened. I asked for an explanation of the content of the activity that occurred. It was a serious problem. Sabotage groups. And we had casualties, fatalities. It's not only water. We'll get water. But what is dangerous is if a sabotage group comes and kills your family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on which date did you ask for these answers and when did he answer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not to go into dates, a response has to be instantaneous, that's done very quickly. If it is an extraordinary situation, requiring an extraordinary interim report, then there has to be urgent action and you cannot postpone things. But when we say interim report, extraordinary report, people make big mistakes, sometimes they treat this as sort of a decision on another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell me what my official position was in relation to the abuse of food supplies, water works, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were a striking example of respect for humaneness and respect for people and humanity as such. It is a great tragedy that you were president in wartime. You were supposed to be president in peacetime so that we could develop like the civilised world. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D104, please, could that be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the date, March 1993, the 11th of March, 1993, to the Main Staff. Could you read paragraph 2? Actually, all of it. Number 1 has to do with the civilian population as well.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. That is you, no interpreters needed here. President, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, this is you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did the Main Staff send this on to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course. And we discussed this at meetings, of course. Well, what would that be like if the Main Staff would forget what you wrote to them? I remember several things, your instructions, how to guide commands and their subordinate units. With such positions of yours, we managed to save ourselves from the paramilitaries, save ourselves, that's true, because this regulates command and control, people know what their responsibility is, and that is indeed important for professional soldiers. All the rest is hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 3850? You were asked or actually your intentions were challenged, the intentions of the corps that you commanded vis-à-vis the enclaves. So can you tell us, can you tell us whether this document is a regular combat report of your deputy, especially paragraph 2, line 2? What is the objective of the Drina Corps, paragraph 2, the first and second lines? To successfully hold the lines reached and continue with preparing the stabilisation of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That means that we should take up the features that are dominant from a military point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a look at the date up there? Is that the 16th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How big was the area of responsibility? How long was the front line towards central Bosnia? You spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 200 kilometres, including Pilica and Donji Podrinje and then including the municipalities of Zvornik, Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many forces did you have around Srebrenica and how many would be engaged and had it been demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had it been demilitarised there wouldn't have been a single soldier there, quite literally. I got carried away and there is this order where I said, Let us all embark upon production. That is to say that these people start working. I claim that with full responsibility, full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page? Let us see what the decision is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This decision, this last part, can you tell us -- actually, you don't have to read it out. What is the essence? What is the objective of the Drina Corps on the 16th of May, 1995? Is it the liquidation of the enclaves and the takeover of the enclaves, or what is written here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in our wildest dreams, takeover, no way, really. To have a separation of the enclaves, and to stop all of these movements, Srebrenica, Zepa, because it wasn't only Srebrenica, Zepa, because then further on it went on to Kladanj and so on. That is the essence of all essences. I said this a hundred times, I'm going to say it now and I'm going to say it tomorrow: Never, never, did I ask for soldiers to enter Srebrenica in a military way. Features were supposed to be taken. So the commander of the Muslim 28th Division would think that he would need 500.000 bullets, he asked for so much, that that couldn't even fit into a depot. It's a good thing he didn't get that. It's a good thing he didn't get that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3958, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since I don't know how much time I have, today you were quoted as having said to the left of Jadar there was no presence of Muslim forces. What is to the left of Jadar?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb villages. It's part of Orahovica, Borovac, Kiprova [phoen], Jasenova, and all the way to the bauxite mine, towards Podravno. Let us take the land register and land survey and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The town of Srebrenica, is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's a misquotation of what was said. Just to clarify that the -- the -- the quote was from the speech and the speech was this: "Let me tell you that with yesterday's dusk, any organised Muslim life to the left of Jadar ceased existing, meaning nothing of Kutuzero, nothing of Bucje, nothing of this old story and nonsense. All of it is over." Just to be clear about what was put -- what was said during the speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the town of Srebrenica is in relation to Jadar, to the left or right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica is on the right, if you look at Jadar, 11 kilometres is the nearest point, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who held the villages to the left of Jadar before the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims for the most part. Muslims for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We are not limiting your time. Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll finish in about five minutes, ten minutes, we can take the break and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that we have only ten minutes of tape that's left. If you can finish in less than ten minutes, we can go on. Otherwise we need to take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I don't do very well when I'm pressed for time. I'm not very efficient. Perhaps it's better to take the break now and then we can continue after the break and be done within 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We shall take a break and resume at 20 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, we saw in that previous document --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can I tender that document of 16 May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have admitted it as D3958.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We saw what the intentions were of the Drina Corps in mid-May. Can you tell us what the situation was on the front line in Republika Srpska, especially in your area, especially in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of June 1995, we had an imminent threat of escalation from these enclaves, that of Srebrenica and that of Zepa, and Gorazde. So there was that fear. Not to mention attacks from the main front. The information we received indeed consisted of warnings that there would be an all-out offensive of Muslim forces against our units and our areas. That is the essence of all documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was not a "yes" or "no" question but your answer was very nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7924, could that document now be shown to the General?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your information about the situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, 97, maybe I made a mistake, 9724.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you remember this report of 15 June 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course, I remember, and this confirms the thoughts I expressed a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that this was still going on, and when did the spring offensive start in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be stated freely that the 14th of June can be taken as the critical date, in terms of intensified combat activities against our areas. However, one should never lose sight of the permanent incursions by sabotage groups in our territory, and that makes it difficult to focus on command and control and fighting on the front line, because this simply never went down on their side, and that is why the enclaves were so good. We have an analysis of their activities in documents and this is absolutely accurate, to the letter. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the situation in other theatres of war, Sarajevo and others?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Continuous operations, continuous preparations. Our units were in contact with the Serb forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. They also conveyed to us that attacks became more and more frequent, attacks, I repeat, because combat in defence is one thing, sabotage is another, but attacking front lines, that is a serious matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now? I believe in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph, ten wounded, four fatalities that day. Can you help us with that? Some of our soldiers were massacred. Can you take a look at this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, heaven forbid, one of our combatants would fall into their hands, then he would be massacred. I wish I could put it differently but unfortunately that was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At this moment, mid-June, do you still -- are you still involved in a counteroffensive or are you just defending yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We soldiers call that active defence. That is to say, repelling enemy forces where they cannot threaten you, at least not in the first stage of combat activities. That's very important. That's the military task involved. New attacks cannot be carried out without more preparation and without more forces involved. That is the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Without taking into account renegade behaviour by individual members of the army, can you tell me, was there a single unit, even the smallest one under the rules of your service, that committed a criminal act according to the rules of planning, decision making and issuing of orders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just when I was talking to Mr. Peter McCloskey, Mrs. Irene Willis and other esteemed ladies and gentlemen who covered these subjects with me, I raised something that is the answer to your question. Not a single, not the lowest ranking smallest unit, not a squad, a battalion, a company or a corps, ever received a single order that goes beyond the framework of well-known conventions that regulate the rules of warfare and conduct in war. I asked them to show me such an order, if it exists, but to this day, nobody has ever been able to produce one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your troops live inside barracks, in barrack conditions and where did your troops live and sleep when they were not on duty?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's well known that from Milici to Tuzla, from Sarajevo to Valjevo, there were no orderly military installations. It was a territory without any military installations, without any military barracks, et cetera. The fighting men who were granted leaves of absence, not long ones, just five, six days, to visit their families, to get a proper bath, a change of clothing, et cetera, all of them went wherever they could get some rest. And the fighting men whose houses had been burned down, they went into collective accommodation or to the houses of their friends and improvised facilities. For instance, there was one such facility in the administration building of the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about your control over the free time of soldiers? To what extent were you able, you in the command, were you able to control how they spent their free time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, there should have been strengthened control measures but we did not have enough staff and we were constantly under pressure to provide more personnel to the front line, more personnel for logistics, to provide the basic prerequisites for a normal life. So the soldiers were not really supervised all the time or lined up regularly, but there was discipline. They had to return to the unit on the date specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How precise were the weapons and the artillery that you had available to you around June 1995, before you entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ZIVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put this question to me as a civilian and I have to answer as a soldier. The weapons were of extremely high precision, but that precision was not abused. I've already said in my evidence earlier today, we did not target roads, we did not target columns of people, we did not target anything other than the combat disposition of enemy formations, and I am a professor of ballistics after all. Our precision was such that we simply couldn't miss. First of all, this is an easily visible terrain. Distances were not great. Artillery weapons were extremely precise. And all our military equipment and technology was extremely precise. Great advances have been made, science has contributed a lot to the military arts, and technology, so if somebody wants to use the full power of such weapons, the losses inflicted are enormous. Nobody should fool themselves that a weapon can miss. People are well-trained now. The weapons are of high quality. And God knows, if somebody gave an improper order, the losses inflicted could be huge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt the translation but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please put a pause before you intervene but I know -- I understand the difficulty, but in particular, Judge Lattanzi has a problem when you intervene --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies. I was trying to get in before the next question just to say that the matters that have been elicited in the answer to that question go well out of the areas which I dealt with in cross-examination, and just to say that any further questioning on the topic of precision of weapons and so on, I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, would you like to respond to this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, absolutely not. The Prosecution raised the matter of the destruction of houses. They claimed, alleged, that the Drina Corps destroyed houses. I asked General Zivanovic if they had T54 tanks, whether they used them, how many houses in Srebrenica they hit. Can a T84 tank hit a window on a house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My questions were about 1993 in relation to that topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- and the question asked was about June 1995, so I would object to that characterisation of my cross. And the question that was put by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, it's the same corps, the same man, and the same doctrine. Why would he be hitting something in 1993 and not hitting the same thing in 1995? There is the singleness of personality and formation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Ms. Pack. The Chamber recommends to you move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other topics. I would finish here with General Zivanovic, with my expressions of gratitude, but I want to know whether he was able to hit windows and to what extent he used his fire power. But if you're not interested, he doesn't have to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit this last document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3959, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think you are interested in recross-examining on the accuracy of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Certainly I'm not. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, unless my colleagues have a question for you, General, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, with your leave, I would like to express my best wishes to you, to the Prosecution and everyone else in this courtroom, to wish you every success in your work, to reduce the antagonisms in our region and to enable our people to live a life worthy of man. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask for two or three minutes for my colleague to replace me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. While the -- we will wait for the next witness to be brought in, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution motion for testimony of Vujadin Popovic to be viva voce, filed on the 21st of October, 2013. In this motion, the Prosecution requests that Vujadin Popovic be led live rather than pursuant to Rule 92 ter, on the basis of his position at the relevant time of the indictment and the significance of his anticipated evidence. The accused filed his response on the 28th of October, 2013, opposing the motion and arguing that Popovic's proposed statement is clear and comprehensible and that Popovic's connections to the accused was, and I quote, "non-existent as compared to those persons for whom viva voce testimony has been ordered." Having reviewed Popovic's proposed Rule 92 ter statement, which is 13 pages with no associated exhibits, as well as having considered Popovic's position as chief of security of the Drina Corps, the Chamber finds that it is appropriate to receive Popovic's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, as originally proposed, and thus denies the Prosecution's request in this respect. However, given the significance of Popovic's testimony, the Chamber has decided to grant the Prosecution's request for three and a half hours for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Kovac. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Could the counsel assisting Mr Kovac introduce himself for record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic, and I will assist Mr Kovac in today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Before you commence your evidence, Mr Kovac, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of Procedure and Evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled in such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr Kovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General -- Mr Kovac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to see if I can see you directly, and also I'd like to remind you to leave a short pause between questions and answers so that everything can be correctly and completely interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following you when you said you could see him directly. Shall I ask Mr. Lazarevic to move his chair? Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull up in e-court, please, the redacted version of 1D09754?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With the Chamber's leave, General, I'd like to ask you, do you have your statement in front of you, in the Serbian language, and if you don't, do you want to have one?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I have it on me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we offer a hard copy to Mr Kovac? 1D09754, the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It hasn't been released, Mr. Karadzic. We're just awaiting -- it hasn't been released. We are awaiting its release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The paper you have in front of you, is it your statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see it on the left side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the last page in e-court, the one with the signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions here and now, would your answers be essentially the same as those given in the statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I tender this 92 ter statement, both the redacted and the unredacted versions. Oh, excuse me, we redacted it on the Chamber's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall deal with the associated exhibits separately. Do you have any objection, Mr. Nicholls, to the admission of statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D9754 will be Exhibit D3960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the associated exhibits, are they all of them on the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has a couple or three observations. First, 1D698, referred to in paragraph 13, Chamber has question about its relevance and its nature that relates -- it's indispensable and inseparable from the statement. And -- just a second. With respect to two appointment documents, i.e. 1D9800 and 65 ter 18495, given that his positions were not challenged, I'm not sure if the Defence need those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We always like to have them to corroborate the witness, but you, in the past, have found them not necessary so we leave it up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So except for those three documents, all the other associated exhibits will be admitted and assigned numbers in due course by the Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do you want my position concerning this first document about food and the two appointment-related documents? Just to explain why we tendered them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you find it necessary, you can deal with it live, showing the relevance. I leave it to you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now read the short summary of General Tomislav Kovac's statement - he's a police general - in English. [In English] General Tomislav Kovac was a professional police officer in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He worked in the Ministry of Interior in Sarajevo, prior to the outbreak of the war, and then served as chief of the police security section in Ilidza. After the war began, he rose in the ranks of the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior and became a minister in September 1995. As the police commander in Ilidza, Tomislav Kovac personally witnessed the activities of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. These organisations targeted Serbs and Serbian residences before the war. On April 22nd, 1992, Ilidza was attacked from the three directions by Muslim forces. The medical rehabilitation centre was seized and 13 Serbs were killed in open fire. Tomislav Kovac never knew of any plan to expel Muslims or Croats from Serb-controlled territory. After the establishment of the Serbian authorities, Muslims and Croats remained in the area of Ilidza and were not disturbed. Following the attack on Ilidza, however, many individuals including Serbs left voluntarily. While there were cases of abuse of Muslim paramilitary groups, the police did not support this and attempted to prevent it. When the Ministry of Interior was consolidated and grew stronger, it reduced the activity of paramilitary groups and investigated crimes against the non-Serbs, all with the support and encouragement of President Karadzic. In July 1995, Tomislav Kovac was Deputy Minister of Interior. During the period from 9th to 20th of July, 1995, General Kovac participated in several meetings with President Karadzic. The main focus of these meetings was the situation around Sarajevo where the Bosnian Muslims had launched an offensive which threatened Serbian communities in the Sarajevo area. During those meetings, Mr. Kovac never heard anything to indicate that the men from Srebrenica would be, were being, or had been executed. He is not aware of any written reports or documents which indicated that prisoners had been executed. President Karadzic issued a series of orders on 10th to 12th July, directing that forces of the Ministry of Interior be engaged in the area of Srebrenica and that a police station be established in Srebrenica to ensure that order and security was maintained there. General Kovac is convinced that President Karadzic had no idea that persons from Srebrenica would be executed. On 14th of July, 1995, General Kovac learned from Ljubomir Borovcanin that an incident had taken place at the Kravica warehouse the evening before, where one policeman had been killed and a detachment commander had been injured in an incident when Muslim prisoners overpowered the policemen who were guarding them. He was also informed that a number of Muslim prisoners were killed in the incident. He never discussed these incidents with President Karadzic. General Kovac was also informed by his subordinates from the Zvornik Public Security Centre that Colonel Beara of the Bosnian Serb Army had requested the assistance of the police with a large number of prisoners from prisoners who were transported to the Zvornik area. They suspected that Beara might want these prisoners killed. When he heard this, Mr. Kovac ordered the police to cease communication with the military security organ and not to be involved in any way in their activities. General Kovac did not discuss this information with President Karadzic. During their meetings in July 1995, President Karadzic never gave any indication that he was aware of the killings of prisoners from Srebrenica. In September 1995, General Kovac tasked some men from the Ministry of Interior to gather information about the allegations that the men from Srebrenica had been executed. He never found any information which indicated that President Karadzic was aware of the existence of a plan to execute the prisoners or had played any role in these executions. General Kovac believes that the crimes in Srebrenica were the worst thing that could have happened to the Serbian people, and he considers the perpetrators of these crimes in Srebrenica as the biggest enemies of the Serbian people itself. And that is short summary. At that moment I will not have additional documents or questions for General Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the summary, and in the statement itself, witness stated that he was appointed as minister in September 1995. But my understanding is that, from a certain point of time, he was acting as the minister while he -- in the capacity of deputy minister. Could you clarify with the witness from when it was like that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Excellency, and explain to you that it was important because the documents about appointments were -- General Kovac was not a politician, a political figure, so it was more difficult, but I can ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you tell us, from what point were you on the acting position and why were the appointments late? Were you a member of a political party? What was the basis for you having to wait a long time on many occasions, that you actually held a certain position but you had to wait a long while until you were officially appointed to it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I was acting minister for the first time in September 1993, up until January 1994. The position of deputy minister was one I held from 1994 until September 1995. I was at the position of deputy minister. In the middle of the year, around the month of July, Minister Rakic simply stopped coming to Pale. He had two offices, one in Banja Luka and another one in Pale. And he simply stopped coming. So I could not state exactly when his function ceased formally. As the deputy minister in operative terms, I had the powers and the authority to manage the MUP in the operational sense. So I cannot even know specifically myself when he ceased to be at this position formally because he was discharging his duty as the minister in two different locations. Perhaps President Karadzic could tell us more precisely when he formally stopped to discharge this duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Chamber whether or how many ministers you had and how many of them were professionals and how many were civilians? What did that look like? Who was first the minister, who was then the second, who was the third? I mean those to whom you were the deputy and then the acting minister, and then you were the fourth, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: We had Minister Stanisic, he was a professional. Then we had Adzic, who was not a professional. We had Rakic, who wasn't a professional. So a total of four of us ministers during the war. While doing my work in a continuity I was, in fact, at the head of the department of public security from the month of August, but at certain points I was also appointed the acting minister. I was forced also to discharge the duties of the deputy minister and I had to manage the MUP in the operational sense. Now, why, even though I did not request this position, why did it all happen so? It was because it was difficult for you in the Assembly to appoint me, not just a priority or political issue, but it was more my question about my attitude towards the local communities and the then-SAO regions which had been constituted. I was expressly a man in favour of centralised authority and certainly many of them saw me as someone who disagreed with their positions and local policies, especially as some of them were frequently processed in one way or another by the services of the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I believe that this will satisfy your request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to Halilovic's book referred to in para 69 of his statement, it will be admitted with respect to only three pages that has been translated, not the entire book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr Kovac, as you have noted, except for the last part, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, i.e. through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr Kovac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We've met before?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to go over quickly your past testimony. This is, if I've got it right, the fifth trial you've testified in; correct? Criminal trial.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You testified in the Medic case, in 2005, in Belgrade. You testified at the BiH State Court in 2007, and in 2010 again. And also in the Zupljanin case, here, in 2012; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you told the truth in your testimony in all those cases, correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were a Court witness in the Zupljanin case, in other words, you were called by the Judges, not by the Prosecutor or the Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember that you, as a Court witness, you were proofed by the Legal Officers for that honourable Trial Chamber? They met with you before your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, nothing important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it was a little important because what they did was they showed you your OTP interviews up to that point, 2003, 2005 and 2010, three times you'd been interviewed by the OTP, up to August 2010, and you told them in the transcript that other than minor translations, as I say, minor errors in terms of names or dates, you stood by your statements in those OTP interviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly so, but as for the assessments which followed from it and the manner they were presented, I did not always agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well that's one thing that's different but let's just keep it simple. You told the truth to the best of your ability in all of your interviews with the OTP, correct, with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, clearly, I always spoke the truth, and I am at your disposal today to talk about specific facts. We can discuss them, I can answer your questions, because the previous part was quite long and the approaches of your investigators were different and the relations between you and the Sarajevo Prosecutor's office, so all of these aspects had an impact on the character of my statements. The facts themselves were never a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just point out that that was a much longer answer than necessary and I'm not trying to be rude to you, but you answered my question, I asked if you always told the truth and you said in the beginning: "Yes, clearly I always spoke the truth." That answered the question. You didn't need to add that extra part. One of the things, and just to go back to what His Honour Judge Kwon raised about your status, you were asked about that in your 2003 interview, your first interview with the -- my office of the Office of the Prosecutor and you were asked, this is at page 24 of the English, I was deputy -- your answer about your status was: "I was deputy minister so there was no need for me to be acting minister because the legal background gave me the authority to be the minister and act on his behalf in case of his absence and things like that. And since I was always number 1 operative, all of those police officers would always think of me as their real boss. You know, the man in charge, rather than the politician who would be brought to the position." So that -- that's correct, isn't it, the police viewed you as their boss, not Mr. Rakic, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Police is not governed in such a way that the leader is elected. I did hold the position of the deputy minister, and in the absence of the minister I had to act operatively because I said that the minister at the time had three seats, one in Bijeljina, for the minister, in Banja Luka, as he was from Krajina, and there was the one that was attached to the government in Pale. So I would not accept an assessment that the police specially elected me. But from the point of view of the law, as long as there was a minister, he was always entitled to be considered as such, and he was entitled to make decisions. Making big political decisions is one thing and running the ministry in the operative sense is something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. There may have been a miscommunication there, but during this time, July 1995, let's say, do you stand by your statement that the police officers would think of you as their real boss, as you told us in 2003?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I cannot claim the right that they considered me their real boss. They accepted me as deputy minister, when the minister was not there they accepted me, that was my legal right and obligation to issue certain instructions and orders, which were, once again in accordance with the law. So it was not on the basis of me being some sort of boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P02981, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've seen this document before. In addition to being deputy minister, as of 19 June, you were head of this MUP police staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: To be precise, this staff was established for the needs of the Sarajevo-Romanija front, and it was -- it only operated with the aim to help with the defence of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the defence of the Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. I didn't ask you what the purpose of the staff was at this point. I asked if you were head of the staff, as it says here. And you are; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly, as I was the head of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let's jump ahead a bit. You talk about your meeting with Mr. Karadzic on 9 July in paragraph 110 of your statement, and your story is that Mr. Karadzic was on the phone with General Krstic, on the speakerphone, and he asked General Krstic what was happening in the Srebrenica operation, and that General Krstic told him that Srebrenica was a sure thing, and this is the part, and that General Krstic -- and that Mr. Karadzic told General Krstic that he, Krstic, should send a request to Karadzic to send two police detachments to Srebrenica. Right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: That's right, but I also said what the reason was; namely that that was needed because we had to maintain the position of the Supreme Commander, to Radovan Karadzic, because he was at that moment in conflict with General Mladic and had no communication with him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And you said that you objected to this, this is in paragraph 112, because your forces were spread out in a thin line in Sarajevo, and you thought that the forces would have a conflict with General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I said I opposed that for two reasons. One were the needs, because objectively speaking, only the Sarajevo front was under threat, and the other thing, it's correct that there would be a conflict of these units or their commanders in the field with General Mladic. I don't mean in military terms but certainly in the manner that the command and control was organised. And I also said that I did not refuse what I never thought or knew that it would happen, that we would have any prisoners of war there and least of all that someone would execute them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You didn't think there would be any prisoners of war. And that is something you've testified about before. This is in the Mitrovic case in 2007. It's at -- 65 ter 25515 is the transcript, page 22. And were you asked by the Defence lawyer in that case about the 10 July order, and the engagement of the MUP in Srebrenica: "Why were you against the engagement of the members of the MUP?" And your answer was: "I opposed this engagement for purely -- namely for operative tactical reasons because I knew that there was no essential reason for the engagement of police units on the Srebrenica front, while on the other hand, on the Sarajevo one, where they were engaged, it was direly needed." So my question is: Do you stand by that answer that you gave under oath in 2007 in court?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I certainly do, because I knew that the incidents which occurred around Srebrenica by the Muslim forces were only linking up of different forces because the war goal was to conquer the Serbian part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So are you aware that as far back as May, VRS plans to liberate, create conditions for the liberation of the enclaves, called for the use of MUP forces? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: As for their plans to liberate the enclaves in May, no, I wasn't aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
